flashcards.q: What's the deliberate order of the five rounds in the full loop, and why that order?
flashcards.a: Coding -> Design -> AI Depth (ML or GenAI) -> Behavioral -> HM Grill. Coding first (mechanically graded, before fatigue). Design second (fresh for 45min of sustained structure). AI depth third (mid-loop, derivation over recall). Behavioral fourth (deliberately after the technical gauntlet, to surface whether STAR discipline survives fatigue). HM grill last (mirrors how real onsites close).

flashcards.q: What's the single core principle of the committee verdict, stated as a rule?
flashcards.a: A candidate does not get hired by being good on average -- they get hired by not being bad anywhere, plus being excellent somewhere. The verdict is not an arithmetic average of the five round scores.

flashcards.q: What's the operative question the committee asks about the weakest round, instead of computing a mean?
flashcards.a: Does the weakest round, on its own, indicate a gap serious enough to sink the hire regardless of the other four -- weighted by how central that round's skill is to the actual role.

flashcards.q: Why is a pattern of contradiction between a strong round and a weak round worse than uniformly middling performance across all five?
flashcards.a: It suggests the strong round may have been well-rehearsed rather than reflecting real depth -- the committee should re-examine the strong round's evidence more skeptically, not just average around the weak one.

flashcards.q: How is the level read (senior/staff/principal) determined from a full loop, and what's the common mistake?
flashcards.a: From the PATTERN across at least 3 of the 5 rounds, not from the single best round. The common mistake is rounding up to the best data point -- if 4 rounds show senior-level structure and only 1 shows a staff-level unprompted tradeoff, the honest read is senior with staff potential, not staff.

flashcards.q: What are the four required elements of the committee verdict, in order?
flashcards.a: 1) Overall recommendation (not an average). 2) The round that would have sunk it, named specifically even in an overall HIRE. 3) The level read with specific supporting evidence and the specific gap to the next level. 4) One thing to fix -- the single highest-leverage gap across all five rounds, not five separate fixes.

flashcards.q: What's the 'consistency check' in the debrief, and what specifically does it look for?
flashcards.a: Whether the same fact, number, or scope claim stays identical across rounds where the same story recurs (e.g. the same headline metric's measurement method described the same way in the behavioral round and the HM grill), and whether seniority signals (unprompted tradeoffs, honest uncertainty) persist into round 4-5 or only appear early.

flashcards.q: What does 'front-loading' look like as a full-loop failure pattern, and why does it read worse than simple fatigue?
flashcards.a: A visibly strong round 1 followed by a collapse in seniority signals (no more unprompted tradeoffs, no more honest uncertainty) by round 4-5. It reads as rehearsed material running out, not fatigue, because genuine depth doesn't have a fixed supply that runs dry after one round.

flashcards.q: Why is referencing an earlier round's content ('I already covered this in the design round') treated as evasive in the full loop, even though it might be true?
flashcards.a: Real interviewers in a real loop have not seen the other rounds' content -- referencing an earlier round instead of answering the current question directly reads as evasive regardless of the candidate's intent.

flashcards.q: What single round outcome is treated as a serious signal regardless of how strong the other four rounds are?
flashcards.a: Any single round scoring STRONG NO HIRE (0-4/20) -- a real committee treats this as a serious, not automatically overridable, signal even against four strong rounds.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the STRONG HIRE and HIRE overall bands, in terms of round distribution?
flashcards.a: STRONG HIRE: no round below HIRE (13+), at least one round at STRONG HIRE (17+) in the domain most relevant to the target role, level read supported by 3+ rounds. HIRE: at most one round at LEAN HIRE (and not in a role-central domain), no round at NO HIRE or below, seniority signals persist (even if less frequently) into later rounds.

flashcards.q: Why should the debrief never be skipped, even after a 4-hour loop?
flashcards.a: Roughly half the module's value lives in the debrief's cross-round consistency check and level-read reasoning -- running all five rounds and skipping straight to an overall verdict without it wastes the harder, more diagnostic half of the exercise.

flashcards.q: How should a bad round be handled going into the next round, both by the interviewer and the candidate?
flashcards.a: Each round is judged on its own evidence -- a bad round's score should not bleed into the next round's scoring. The candidate's failure mode to avoid: spending the next round's early minutes mentally re-litigating the previous bad round instead of resetting and being present for the new prompt.

flashcards.q: What's the cross-cutting rubric dimension this module adds on top of the five rounds' own 20-point rubrics?
flashcards.a: Consistency across rounds -- scored separately and reported alongside the five round scores, checking whether facts/numbers/scope claims stay identical across rounds and whether seniority signals persist at the same rate in round 5 as round 1.

flashcards.q: Why is a LEAN HIRE in the role's core skill weighted worse than a STRONG HIRE somewhere less central to the role?
flashcards.a: The committee verdict weights the weakest round by its relevance to the actual job -- a LEAN HIRE on GenAI depth for a GenAI-heavy role is a bigger problem than a LEAN HIRE on coding for a role that's 90% design and stakeholder work, even if the raw scores look similar.
